title: Story Elements
bigQuestion: What are the parts every story is built from, and how do you find them?

story.title: Tops and Bottoms
story.kicker: A hungry rabbit, a lazy bear, and one question that turns the whole story around.
paragraphs: Bear owned a big field but hated to work. Rabbit owned nothing but had six hungry kids. One spring Rabbit knocked on Bear's door. "Let me farm your field," he said. "I will do all the work. You just pick which half of each crop you want, the tops or the bottoms." Bear yawned. "Tops," he said, and went back to sleep.

Rabbit planted carrots. He watered, he weeded, he pulled. In the fall he brought Bear a wagon of leafy green tops. Bear got a wagon of leaves. Rabbit's kids got a winter of sweet orange carrots. Bear was angry. "Next year I want the bottoms!"

So Rabbit planted lettuce. In the fall Bear got a wagon of roots and dirt. Rabbit's family ate crisp lettuce all season. Bear roared. "Next year I take the tops AND the bottoms!" Rabbit only nodded, and planted corn.

When Mr. Okafor's class read this tale, he stopped and asked, "Where does the story turn?" Hands went up. Some said the corn. Some said the roar. Then Jada said, "It turns the first time Rabbit asks 'tops or bottoms?' That is when we know he has a plan." Mr. Okafor smiled. She had found the moment the whole story hangs on.

By the third harvest, Bear got a wagon of corn tassels and a wagon of roots. Rabbit's family got the ears of corn, the part in the middle. Bear finally decided to farm the field himself. That, the tale says, is how Bear learned to work.
story.think: Jada said the story turns on a question. Do you agree? Where would you say the turning point is, and why?

lessons.title: Traits Show in Actions
lessons.mainIdea: A character trait is what a character is like, and you find it by watching what the character does and says.
reading: Read this: "Marisol saw the new kid eating alone. She picked up her tray and walked over. 'Can I sit here?' she asked." Nobody says Marisol is kind. But you know it. You saw what she did.

What a person is like is called a *trait*. Kind, brave, lazy, sneaky, and honest are traits. In a story, a writer rarely tells you a trait straight out. Instead the writer shows an *action*. You read the action and name the trait yourself. That is your job as a reader.

Try it with Bear from the tale. He owns a field but will not plant it. He says "tops" and goes back to sleep. Those actions add up. Bear is lazy. Rabbit works all season and thinks ahead. Rabbit is clever and hard-working. Every trait you name should come from something the character actually did.

words.d: a word that tells what a character is like, such as kind, lazy or brave
something a character does in the story

look.title: Two Kids, One Dropped Wallet
look.text: Tomas finds a wallet on the bus floor. He looks around, then slides it into his backpack. Across the aisle, Lena finds a phone. She walks it up to the driver and says, "Somebody lost this."
look.prompt: Name one trait for Tomas and one for Lena. What action did you use for each one?

check.q: How do you usually find out a character's trait?
choices: The writer lists the traits at the start
You watch what the character does and says
check.why: Writers show actions. Readers name the trait from those actions.

check.q: Which word is a trait?
check.why: Honest tells what a person is like. The others name things or days.

check.q: Bear sleeps while Rabbit farms the field. What trait does that action show?
check.why: Bear will not work his own field. That action shows he is lazy.

lessons.title: Why Characters Act
lessons.mainIdea: A motive is the reason a character does something, and feelings often change what a character decides to do.
reading: Why did Rabbit knock on Bear's door? He was not being friendly. He had six hungry kids and no field. That reason is his *motive*. A motive is the reason behind an action. Ask "why did she do that?" and you are looking for a motive.

Feelings drive motives too. A character who is scared may hide or run. A character who is angry may shout something she regrets. Bear roared "tops AND bottoms" because he *felt* cheated. His anger made him greedy, and greed made him easy to trick again.

Writers give clues to feelings without naming them. "Her hands shook. She stared at the floor." Nobody said nervous, but you know. Clues like shaking hands, a tight voice, or a slammed door tell you the feeling. Then the feeling helps you guess the motive for what the character does next.

words.d: the reason a character does something
an emotion such as fear, anger, joy or shame that a character has

look.title: A Motive Hidden in Plain Sight
look.text: Devon offered to walk the neighbor's dog every day for free. His mom was surprised. Devon did not say that the dog lived next door to a girl named Kaya, or that Kaya was usually outside at four o'clock.
look.cite: model text, written for this lesson
look.prompt: What is Devon's real motive? What clue gives it away?

check.q: What is a motive?
choices: The reason a character does something
check.why: A motive is the why behind an action.

check.q: Rabbit knocks on Bear's door. What is his motive?
choices: He wants to be Bear's friend
He wants to sell carrots to Bear
He needs to feed his six kids
check.why: Rabbit has hungry kids and no field. Feeding them is why he acts.

check.q: "Her hands shook. She stared at the floor." What feeling do these clues show?
check.why: Shaking hands and looking down are clues to nervousness or fear.

lessons.title: When a Character Changes
lessons.mainIdea: Many characters are different at the end of a story than at the start, and the change usually comes from what happens to them.
reading: At the start of the tale, Bear will not lift a paw. At the end, he farms his own field. That is a *change*. Bear is not the same bear. Stories about a character who changes are everywhere, because change is what makes a story feel finished.

To track a change, take two snapshots. Snapshot one: what is the character like on page one? Snapshot two: what is he like on the last page? Then ask what happened in between. For Bear, three harvests of leaves and roots taught him a lesson he could not sleep through.

Not every character changes. Rabbit is clever at the start and clever at the end. He is the same. A character who stays the same is called *static*. A character who changes is *dynamic*. When you read, watch for the character who is different at the end. That is usually the one the story is about.

words.d: when a character is different at the end of a story than at the start
a character who stays the same through the whole story
a character who changes because of what happens in the story

look.title: Snapshot One, Snapshot Two
look.text: Page one: Ines refuses to try out for the play. "I will forget every line," she says. Last page: Ines stands on stage in a paper crown, bowing while the crowd claps. Between those pages, her big brother ran lines with her every night for two weeks.
look.prompt: What changed in Ines? What happened in the middle that caused the change?

check.q: Which character in the tale is dynamic?
choices: Rabbit, who is clever all the way through
Bear, who is lazy at first and works at the end
check.why: Bear changes. He starts lazy and ends up farming. That makes him dynamic.

check.q: What does it mean if a character is static?
choices: The character is the main one
check.why: Static means the character does not change during the story.

check.q: What is the best way to track a character's change?
choices: Count how many times the name appears
Skip the middle of the story
Compare the character at the start and at the end
check.why: Two snapshots, start and end, show the change. Then look for the cause in between.

lessons.title: Setting Is Time and Place
lessons.mainIdea: The setting is where and when a story happens, and it shapes what the characters can and cannot do.
reading: "Snow piled against the cabin door. The lamp was almost out of oil." Two sentences, and you already know a lot. It is winter. It is night, or nearly. There is no electricity. This is the *setting*: where and when the story happens.

Setting is not just a background. It changes what can happen. In a snowed-in cabin, a character cannot call for help or run to a store. In a Chicago apartment in July, the problem might be a broken fan and a hot night. Move the same character to a new setting and the story changes with her.

Writers give setting through *details*: the weather, the light, the sounds, the year, the objects around. A story with a horse and a candle is probably set long ago. A story with a bus pass and a phone is set now. Collect the details, and the setting comes into focus.

words.d: where and when a story takes place
a small, specific piece of information, like the weather or an object in the room

look.title: One Sentence, Many Clues
look.text: "Amara pulled her scarf over her nose and waited for the Red Line, stamping her boots on the platform while the wind came off the lake." Read it twice. Look for the season, the city, and the time of day if you can find it.
look.prompt: What is the setting? Which details told you? Is there anything you cannot tell yet?

check.q: What two things does a setting tell you?
check.why: Setting is the place and the time of a story.

check.q: A story has a horse, a candle and a wooden wagon. What can you guess about the setting?
choices: It is set in a big city today
It is set on the moon
It is set in a school
check.why: Candles and wagons are details that point to an earlier time.

check.q: Why does setting matter to the plot?
choices: It tells the reader the ending
It changes what the characters are able to do
check.why: A snowed-in cabin and a city block give characters very different choices.

lessons.title: The Shape of a Plot
lessons.mainIdea: A plot moves from a problem, through events, to a climax, and then to a solution.
reading: Rabbit has no field and hungry kids. That is the *problem*. He makes a deal, plants carrots, plants lettuce, plants corn. Those are the events. Bear roars "tops AND bottoms!" and Rabbit still finds a way. That is the *climax*, the most exciting moment. Bear gives up and farms for himself. That is the *solution*. You just read a whole plot in four sentences.

Almost every story follows this shape. First a problem shows up. Then events pile on and the problem gets harder. Then comes the climax, the turning point where things are most tense. After it, the story slides toward a solution and the ending. Picture a hill: up, up, the top, then down.

Knowing the shape helps you read. When you feel lost in a story, ask: "What is the problem? Has the climax happened yet?" If the character is still struggling, you are on the way up. If things are settling down, you are past the top. This works for a picture book and for a long novel.

words.d: the trouble a character faces that starts the story moving
the most exciting or tense moment of a story, where things turn
how the problem gets settled at the end of a story

look.title: Where the Story Spends Its Time
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the chapter's opening tale
look.prompt: The middle harvests get the most space. Why is the middle of a story usually the longest part?

check.q: In which order do the parts of a plot usually come?
check.why: The problem starts it, events build, the climax turns it, and the solution ends it.

check.q: What is the climax of a story?
check.why: The climax is the top of the hill, where things are most exciting and turn.

check.q: A character is still struggling and the trouble keeps growing. Where are you in the plot?
check.why: Growing trouble means you are on the way up the hill, before the climax.

lessons.title: Three Kinds of Trouble
lessons.mainIdea: A conflict is the struggle in a story, and it can be against another character, against nature, or inside the character's own mind.
reading: Rabbit against Bear. A girl against a blizzard. A boy against his own fear of the diving board. All three are stories, and all three have a struggle at the center. That struggle is the *conflict*. No conflict, no story. If nothing pushes back, there is nothing to read about.

The first kind is character against character. Two people want different things, like Rabbit and Bear both wanting the crop. The second kind is character against nature: a storm, a flood, a long cold winter, a mountain. The character cannot argue with a blizzard. She can only find a way through.

The third kind happens inside. Character against *self* means the fight is in the character's own mind. Should I tell the truth? Can I make myself jump? These stories can feel the most real, because you have had that fight too. Many stories mix kinds. A boy lost in the woods may battle the cold and his own panic at the same time.

words.d: the struggle or problem at the center of a story
a character's own mind and feelings; a conflict against self happens inside

look.title: Sort the Struggles
look.text: Story A: Two sisters fight over who gets the top bunk. Story B: A kayaker's boat flips in cold river water and she has to reach the bank. Story C: Malik knows he broke the window, and nobody saw, and he cannot decide whether to say so.
look.prompt: Which kind of conflict is in each story? Which one do you think would be hardest to live through?

check.q: A hiker is trapped by a snowstorm on a mountain. What kind of conflict is this?
check.why: The hiker is struggling against the weather, which is nature.

check.q: Malik cannot decide whether to admit he broke the window. What kind of conflict is this?
check.why: The fight is inside Malik's own mind. That is character against self.

check.q: Why does a story need a conflict?
choices: Without a struggle there is nothing to read about
check.why: The struggle is what pulls a reader through. Something has to push back.

lessons.title: What Dialogue Shows
lessons.mainIdea: Dialogue is the words characters say, and it reveals who they are and what they want without the writer telling you.
reading: "Give it back." "Make me." Two lines, four words, and you already know these two are fighting and neither one will back down. Words that characters say out loud are *dialogue*. Quotation marks show where the spoken words start and stop.

Dialogue does more than fill space. It shows traits. A character who says "Whatever, I don't care" shows one thing. A character who says "Wait, let me help you carry that" shows another. It shows feelings, too. Short, sharp lines can mean anger. Long, rambling lines can mean nerves.

Dialogue can also move the plot. In the tale, Bear says one word, "tops," and that single word decides the whole first harvest. When you read, slow down at the quotation marks. Ask: what does this line tell me about the person saying it? What does it make happen next?

words.d: the words characters say out loud in a story, shown with quotation marks
the marks " " that go around spoken words

look.title: Same Question, Two Answers
look.text: The coach asked who wanted to take the last shot. "I got it," Ray said, already reaching for the ball. Priya looked at her shoes. "I mean, I could, if nobody else wants to."
look.cite: model text, written for this lesson
look.prompt: What does each line of dialogue show about Ray and about Priya? Point to the exact words.

check.q: What is dialogue?
choices: The place where a story happens
The words characters say out loud
check.why: Dialogue is the characters' spoken words, marked with quotation marks.

check.q: "Wait, let me help you carry that." What trait does this line show?
check.why: Offering to carry something shows the character is helpful.

check.q: How can one line of dialogue move the plot?
choices: It cannot; only actions move the plot
It tells the reader the setting
What a character says can decide what happens next
check.why: Bear's one word, "tops," decided the whole first harvest.

lessons.title: Summarize in a Few Sentences
lessons.mainIdea: A summary retells only the main character, the problem, the big events and the ending, in your own words and in order.
reading: A friend missed the movie and asks what happened. You do not repeat every line. You say who it was about, what went wrong, and how it ended. That short retelling is a *summary*. A good summary is short, in order, and in your own words.

Here is a summary of the chapter's tale: "Rabbit has no field, so he farms Bear's land and lets Bear pick tops or bottoms. Each year Rabbit plants a crop that gives Bear the useless half. After three harvests, Bear gives up and farms for himself." Three sentences. Character, problem, events, ending.

Watch out for two mistakes. One is retelling too much: every carrot, every wagon. The other is giving your *opinion*: "It was funny." A summary is not a review. Leave out what you think and keep only what happened. A test: could someone who never read the story follow your summary? If yes, it works.

words.d: a short retelling of the main parts of a story, in order and in your own words
what you personally think or feel about something

look.title: Three Retellings, Three Lengths
look.cite: counted for this lesson; the tale is the chapter's opening story without the classroom paragraph
look.prompt: The good summary is about one-fifth of the tale. What has to be left out to get it that short, and what has to stay?

check.q: Which of these belongs in a summary?
choices: The main problem and how it was solved
check.why: A summary keeps the main character, problem, big events and ending. Details and opinions stay out.

check.q: "This story was boring but the corn part was okay." What is wrong with this as a summary?
choices: It is in the wrong order
It gives an opinion instead of what happened
check.why: A summary tells what happened. Boring and okay are opinions.

check.q: What is a good test for a summary?
choices: Someone who never read the story could follow it
It is at least a full page
It uses the exact words of the book
check.why: If a stranger can follow it, the summary has the parts that matter.

lessons.title: Prove It From the Page
lessons.mainIdea: When you explain a story, back up your idea with evidence: the exact words or events from the text that show it.
reading: "Bear is lazy." Okay, says your teacher, prove it. You flip to the tale and read: "Bear owned a big field but hated to work." Now it is not just your idea. It is on the page. Words or events from the text that support an idea are called *evidence*.

Evidence turns a guess into an answer. Two students can disagree about a character. The one who can point to the page wins the argument. When you write about a story, use a pattern. Say your idea. Give the evidence. Then explain how the evidence proves the idea.

Try this frame: "I think ___. In the text it says '___.' This shows ___." For example: "I think Rabbit plans ahead. In the text it says he 'only nodded, and planted corn.' This shows he already knew what Bear would ask for." Short, clear, and backed by the page. That is what teachers mean when they say *support* your answer.

words.d: words or events from the text that support an idea about the story
to back up an idea with evidence from the text

look.title: Who Made the Better Case?
look.text: Dani says, "Rabbit is sneaky because I just think he is." Luis says, "Rabbit is sneaky. The text says he 'only nodded, and planted corn' right after Bear asked for both halves. He did not warn Bear at all." The class votes on who made the stronger case.
look.prompt: Who wins the vote, and why? What did Luis do that Dani did not?

check.q: What is text evidence?
choices: Words or events from the story that support an idea
check.why: Evidence is what the page actually says or shows.

check.q: Which sentence uses evidence to support an idea?
choices: Bear is lazy because I think so
Bear is lazy and that is that
Bear is lazy; the text says he 'hated to work'
check.why: Only that answer points to the exact words on the page.

check.q: What is the order of a good evidence answer?
choices: Explain, then idea, then the title
Idea, evidence, then explain how it proves the idea
check.why: I think, the text says, this shows. That is the pattern.

lessons.title: Fables and Their Lessons
lessons.mainIdea: A fable is a very short story, usually with animal characters, that ends with a lesson about how to live.
reading: A hare laughs at a tortoise for being slow. They race. The hare naps halfway, sure he will win. The tortoise keeps plodding and crosses the line first. You know this one. It is a *fable*: a short story, often with animals who talk, that teaches a lesson.

The lesson at the end of a fable is called the *moral*. In the race story, the moral is that steady effort beats careless speed. Many fables are said to come from Aesop. He was a storyteller in ancient Greece more than two thousand years ago. Nobody is sure what Aesop was really like. But the stories with his name traveled all over the world.

Fables work because the animals stand for people. The hare is every show-off who thinks the job is done. The tortoise is every kid who keeps going. When you read a fable, ask two questions. What does each animal stand for? What is the story telling me to do, or not do? Answer those and you have the moral.

words.d: a very short story, often with talking animals, that teaches a lesson
the lesson a fable teaches, often stated at the end

look.title: The Lion and the Mouse
look.text: In one of Aesop's best-known fables, a lion catches a mouse and then lets it go, laughing at the idea that something so small could ever repay him. Later the lion is caught in a hunter's net. The mouse chews through the ropes and sets him free.
look.cite: retold from Aesop's fables (ancient Greece), told here in our own words
look.prompt: What is the moral of this fable? What does the mouse stand for?

check.q: What is a moral?
choices: The first line of a story
check.why: The moral is the lesson at the end, the thing the fable wants you to learn.

check.q: Why do fables often use animals instead of people?
choices: The animals stand for kinds of people
Animals cannot talk in real life
check.why: The hare stands for show-offs and the tortoise for steady workers.

check.q: What is the moral of the tortoise and the hare?
check.why: The tortoise kept going. The hare stopped to nap and lost.

lessons.title: Folktales and Myths Worldwide
lessons.mainIdea: Folktales and myths are old stories passed down by many people, and each culture's stories carry that culture's ideas about how to live.
reading: Nobody wrote the first version of Tops and Bottoms. People told it, and their children told it. It changed a little each time. A story passed down by telling is a *folktale*. Rabbit tales like it were told by enslaved African Americans in the South. Clever-rabbit stories also appear in West Africa, in Native American nations, and in Asia. A small, weak animal who wins by wits shows up almost everywhere.

A *myth* is an old story that explains something big. How did the world begin? Why do seasons change? What are the gods like? In a Greek myth, a boy named Icarus flies on wings of wax and feathers. He flies too near the sun. The wax melts, and he falls. That story explained no weather, but it warned every listener about pride.

Reading stories from many cultures shows you two things. First, people everywhere want the same things: food, safety, fairness, a good laugh at a bully. Second, each culture tells it in its own way, with its own animals, foods and places. When you read a folktale, ask: what did the people who told this care about? The answer is usually the lesson.

words.d: an old story passed down by telling, with no single known author
an old story, often with gods, that explains something about the world
the way of life, beliefs and stories shared by a group of people

look.title: The Same Trick, Two Places
look.text: In one tale, a spider named Anansi from West Africa tricks a bigger animal out of its food by asking a clever question. In another, a rabbit in the American South does almost the same thing to a fox. The animals are different. The trick, and the lesson, are nearly the same.
look.prompt: Why might people in two faraway places tell almost the same story? What did both groups seem to care about?

check.q: How is a folktale different from a story in a new book?
choices: Folktales were passed down by telling, with no single author
check.why: A folktale is handed down by many tellers. A new book has one author.

check.q: What does a myth usually do?
choices: Explains something big, like the seasons or the gods
check.why: Myths explain the world and the gods in story form.

check.q: What lesson does the story of Icarus warn about?
choices: Pride can lead to a fall
check.why: Icarus flew too high because he was proud. The myth warns against that.

review.q: A character gives her lunch to a kid who forgot his. What trait does the action show?
review.why: Sharing food is a generous action.

review.q: The reason a character does something is called the
review.why: A motive is the why behind an action.

review.q: Which part of a plot comes right after the climax?
review.why: After the turning point, the story heads to the solution.

review.q: "Snow piled against the cabin door. The lamp was almost out of oil." What is this mostly telling you?
review.why: Snow, a cabin and a lamp are details of place and time, the setting.

review.q: A boy cannot decide whether to tell the truth. Which conflict is this?
review.why: The struggle is inside his own mind.

review.q: What should a summary leave out?
review.why: A summary keeps what happened and leaves out what you think of it.

review.q: "I think Bear is lazy. The text says he 'hated to work.'" What is the second sentence?
review.why: Quoting the page to back up an idea is evidence.

choices: A true story about a real person
A long book with many chapters
A story that explains where the sun came from
A short story with animals that teaches a lesson
review.why: Fables are short, often use animals, and end with a moral.
